causes: Viral or bacterial infections such as flu, COVID-19, or urinary tract infections
Inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease
Heat exhaustion or prolonged sun exposure
self_care: Rest adequately and drink plenty of fluids like water, oral rehydration solution, or clear broths to prevent dehydration
Take over-the-counter antipyretics such as paracetamol (acetaminophen) or ibuprofen as directed on the label
Wear light, breathable clothing and use a lukewarm sponge bath to help bring temperature down
see_doctor_if: Fever persists for more than 3 days or keeps returning after temporarily subsiding
Temperature exceeds 39.4°C (103°F) in adults or is accompanied by severe headache, stiff neck, or unexplained rash
emergency_if: Fever is accompanied by confusion, difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, or seizures
Infant younger than 3 months has a rectal temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher

causes: Upper respiratory viral infections such as the common cold or influenza
Allergies, postnasal drip, or exposure to environmental irritants like smoke or dust
Acid reflux (GERD) causing irritation of the throat and airways
self_care: Stay well-hydrated with warm liquids like honey-lemon water or herbal tea to soothe the throat
Use a humidifier or inhale steam from a bowl of hot water to moisten airways and loosen mucus
Suck on throat lozenges or hard candy and avoid known irritants such as cigarette smoke
see_doctor_if: Cough persists for more than 3 weeks or produces thick green, yellow, or blood-tinged mucus
Cough is accompanied by unexplained weight loss, night sweats, or a persistent low-grade fever
emergency_if: Coughing up significant amounts of blood or blood-streaked sputum
Sudden severe shortness of breath, wheezing, or inability to speak in full sentences

causes: Infection by rhinoviruses, which spread through airborne droplets or contaminated surfaces
Weakened immune defenses from lack of sleep, high stress, or poor nutrition
Close contact with infected individuals, especially in crowded or enclosed spaces
self_care: Rest as much as possible and increase fluid intake to keep mucous membranes moist
Use saline nasal spray or drops to relieve nasal congestion and flush out irritants
Gargle with warm salt water to soothe a sore throat and take OTC decongestants if needed
see_doctor_if: Symptoms worsen after 7-10 days or are accompanied by a high fever above 39°C (102°F)
You develop ear pain, severe sinus pressure, or a persistent productive cough suggesting a secondary bacterial infection
emergency_if: Sudden difficulty breathing, persistent chest tightness, or bluish discoloration of lips
High fever with severe headache, stiff neck, or confusion suggesting meningitis

causes: Tension from stress, poor posture, eye strain, or prolonged screen use
Dehydration, skipped meals, lack of sleep, or excessive caffeine consumption
Migraine triggered by hormonal changes, certain foods, bright lights, or weather shifts
self_care: Take an OTC pain reliever such as paracetamol or ibuprofen and rest in a quiet, dimly lit room
Apply a cold or warm compress to the forehead or neck and gently massage the temples
Drink water to rehydrate and practice relaxation techniques like deep breathing or gentle stretching
see_doctor_if: Headaches become more frequent or severe over weeks, or usual pain medications stop working
Headache follows a head injury or is accompanied by fever, stiff neck, or vision changes
emergency_if: Sudden, extremely severe 'thunderclap' headache that reaches peak intensity within seconds
Headache with confusion, weakness on one side of the body, slurred speech, or loss of consciousness

causes: Indigestion, gas, bloating, or overeating rich and spicy foods
Gastritis, acid reflux (GERD), or peptic ulcers aggravated by stress or NSAIDs
Food intolerance (e.g., lactose intolerance) or mild food poisoning
self_care: Eat small, bland meals (rice, toast, bananas) and avoid spicy, fatty, or acidic foods temporarily
Sip clear fluids like water or ginger tea and try an OTC antacid for acid-related discomfort
Apply a warm compress or heating pad to the abdomen and rest in a comfortable position
see_doctor_if: Pain persists for more than 48 hours, keeps recurring, or is accompanied by unexplained weight loss
You notice blood in your stool, persistent vomiting, or pain that wakes you from sleep
emergency_if: Sudden, severe abdominal pain with a rigid or board-like abdomen suggesting perforation or peritonitis
Abdominal pain with high fever, vomiting blood, or signs of shock such as rapid pulse and clammy skin

causes: Viral gastroenteritis (stomach flu) caused by rotavirus, norovirus, or similar pathogens
Bacterial infection from contaminated food or water (e.g., Salmonella, E. coli)
Food intolerance, medication side effects (especially antibiotics), or stress
self_care: Drink oral rehydration solution (ORS), clear broths, or water frequently to replace lost fluids and electrolytes
Follow the BRAT diet (bananas, rice, applesauce, toast) and avoid dairy, caffeine, and greasy foods
Take OTC loperamide for symptom relief if no fever or bloody stools are present
see_doctor_if: Diarrhea lasts more than 2 days in adults or 24 hours in children, or is accompanied by a fever above 39°C
Signs of dehydration appear: very dry mouth, little or no urination, severe weakness, or dizziness
emergency_if: Bloody or black tarry stools, or diarrhea accompanied by severe abdominal cramping and high fever
Signs of severe dehydration: sunken eyes, inability to keep any fluids down, or altered consciousness

causes: Food poisoning, viral gastroenteritis, or overeating and excessive alcohol consumption
Motion sickness, pregnancy-related morning sickness, or medication side effects
Migraine, strong emotional stress, or inner-ear disorders like labyrinthitis
self_care: Sip small amounts of clear fluids (water, ORS, diluted ginger ale) every 15 minutes to stay hydrated
Avoid solid food until vomiting stops, then reintroduce bland items like crackers, rice, or plain toast
Rest in an upright or side-lying position and avoid strong odors that may trigger nausea
see_doctor_if: Vomiting persists for more than 24 hours in adults or 12 hours in children, preventing any fluid intake
Vomiting is accompanied by severe abdominal pain, headache, stiff neck, or high fever
emergency_if: Vomiting blood (bright red or coffee-ground appearance) or vomiting after a head injury
Signs of severe dehydration: no urination for 8+ hours, rapid heartbeat, confusion, or fainting

causes: Viral infections such as influenza, COVID-19, or dengue that cause systemic inflammation
Overexertion, strenuous exercise, or poor ergonomics during prolonged sitting or standing
Stress and tension causing muscle tightness, or early signs of conditions like fibromyalgia
self_care: Rest the affected muscles and apply alternating warm and cold compresses to reduce pain and inflammation
Take OTC pain relievers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen and stay well-hydrated
Perform gentle stretching exercises and ensure adequate sleep to support muscle recovery
see_doctor_if: Body aches persist beyond a week without improvement or are accompanied by joint swelling and stiffness
Pain is localized, severe, or associated with unexplained weight loss, fever, or night sweats
emergency_if: Sudden severe muscle pain with dark-colored urine suggesting rhabdomyolysis
Body aches with high fever, rash, and stiff neck, which may indicate meningitis or sepsis

causes: Allergic reaction to foods, medications, detergents, cosmetics, or plant contact (e.g., poison ivy)
Viral infections such as chickenpox, measles, or hand-foot-and-mouth disease
Fungal infections (ringworm, athlete's foot), eczema, or contact dermatitis
self_care: Keep the area clean and dry, apply a fragrance-free moisturizer, and avoid scratching to prevent secondary infection
Use OTC hydrocortisone cream (1%) or calamine lotion to relieve itching and inflammation
Take an oral antihistamine like cetirizine or diphenhydramine if itching is widespread
see_doctor_if: Rash spreads rapidly, does not improve within a week, or is accompanied by fever and joint pain
Rash shows signs of infection: increasing warmth, swelling, pus, or red streaks spreading from the area
emergency_if: Rash appears suddenly with difficulty breathing, throat swelling, or dizziness suggesting anaphylaxis
Widespread blistering, peeling skin, or painful rash around the eyes and mouth (possible Stevens-Johnson syndrome)

causes: Musculoskeletal strain from heavy lifting, coughing, or sudden movements
Acid reflux (GERD) or esophageal spasm causing a burning sensation behind the breastbone
Anxiety or panic attacks that mimic cardiac symptoms with rapid heartbeat and tightness
self_care: If pain is clearly related to muscle strain, rest the area and apply a warm compress gently
For suspected acid reflux, take an OTC antacid and avoid lying down immediately after eating
Practice slow, deep breathing if the chest tightness seems anxiety-related, and try to stay calm
see_doctor_if: Chest pain recurs with exertion, lasts more than a few minutes, or is a new and unexplained symptom
Pain is accompanied by persistent cough, difficulty swallowing, or unexplained weight loss
emergency_if: Crushing or squeezing chest pain radiating to the jaw, left arm, or back — call emergency services immediately
Chest pain with sudden shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or loss of consciousness

causes: Asthma exacerbation triggered by allergens, cold air, exercise, or respiratory infections
Anxiety or panic attacks causing hyperventilation and a sensation of air hunger
Respiratory infections such as pneumonia, bronchitis, or COVID-19 affecting the lungs
self_care: Sit upright in a comfortable position and practice slow, pursed-lip breathing to regulate airflow
Use a prescribed rescue inhaler (e.g., salbutamol) if you have known asthma, following your action plan
Remove yourself from potential triggers like smoke, allergens, or dusty environments and get fresh air
see_doctor_if: Shortness of breath worsens gradually over days, occurs with mild activity, or disrupts sleep
You need to use your rescue inhaler more than twice a week or your peak flow readings are dropping
emergency_if: Severe breathlessness at rest, inability to speak in full sentences, or blue/grey discoloration of lips and fingertips
Sudden onset of breathing difficulty with chest pain, especially after prolonged immobility (possible pulmonary embolism)

causes: Sudden drop in blood pressure (orthostatic hypotension) from standing up too quickly
Inner-ear disorders such as benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) or labyrinthitis
Dehydration, low blood sugar, anemia, or side effects of medications like blood pressure drugs
self_care: Sit or lie down immediately when feeling dizzy and avoid sudden head movements
Drink water or a sugary beverage if dehydration or low blood sugar is suspected
Rise slowly from sitting or lying positions, and avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until symptoms pass
see_doctor_if: Dizziness is recurrent, lasts more than a few days, or is accompanied by hearing loss or ringing in the ears
Episodes occur with fainting, persistent imbalance, or after starting a new medication
emergency_if: Dizziness with sudden severe headache, vision changes, slurred speech, or limb weakness (possible stroke)
Fainting with irregular heartbeat, chest pain, or after a head injury

causes: Poor sleep quality, chronic sleep deprivation, or irregular sleep schedules
High stress, burnout, depression, or anxiety affecting energy levels
Nutritional deficiencies (iron, vitamin B12, vitamin D), anemia, or thyroid disorders
self_care: Prioritize 7-9 hours of quality sleep per night with a consistent bedtime routine
Eat balanced meals with iron-rich foods, whole grains, and fresh fruits and vegetables, and stay hydrated
Incorporate moderate exercise like walking 30 minutes daily and take short breaks during work
see_doctor_if: Fatigue persists for more than 2 weeks despite adequate rest, nutrition, and stress management
Accompanied by unexplained weight change, persistent low-grade fever, or excessive thirst and urination
emergency_if: Sudden extreme fatigue with chest pain, shortness of breath, or irregular heartbeat
Fatigue with confusion, inability to stay awake, or yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice)

causes: Food allergens such as peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, eggs, or dairy products
Insect stings or bites from bees, wasps, or fire ants triggering an immune response
Medications (e.g., penicillin, NSAIDs), latex, or environmental allergens like pollen and pet dander
self_care: Take an OTC oral antihistamine such as cetirizine or loratadine for mild hives, sneezing, or itching
Apply a cold compress to localized swelling or itchy areas and avoid further contact with the suspected allergen
For mild nasal allergy symptoms, use a saline nasal rinse and stay in a clean, well-ventilated environment
see_doctor_if: Allergic symptoms recur frequently, interfere with daily life, or do not respond to OTC antihistamines
You develop swelling of the face, lips, or tongue, or experience stomach cramps and vomiting after exposure
emergency_if: Signs of anaphylaxis: throat tightness, difficulty breathing, rapid pulse, dizziness, or collapse — use epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) and call emergency services
Widespread hives with wheezing, drop in blood pressure, or loss of consciousness

causes: Kitchen accidents involving knives, graters, or hot surfaces, oil splashes, and steam
Scrapes and abrasions from falls, sports activities, or contact with rough surfaces
Minor thermal burns from touching hot utensils, irons, or brief contact with open flames
self_care: For cuts: clean the wound gently with running water, apply antiseptic, and cover with a sterile adhesive bandage
For burns: cool the area under cool (not ice-cold) running water for at least 10 minutes, then cover loosely with a sterile non-stick dressing
Apply an OTC antibiotic ointment to cuts to prevent infection and take OTC pain relief if needed
see_doctor_if: A cut is deep, gaping, won't stop bleeding after 10 minutes of direct pressure, or may need stitches
A burn is larger than 3 inches, blisters significantly, or is located on the face, hands, feet, or joints
emergency_if: Severe uncontrolled bleeding that soaks through bandages, or a deep wound exposing bone or tendon
Large or deep burn with charred or white/waxy skin (third-degree), or burn caused by chemicals or electricity
